Getting a second opinion

A second opinion is normal and your right. Good doctors welcome it. It can confirm your diagnosis and plan, or find options you did not know about.

When a second opinion makes sense

  • You have a new cancer diagnosis, a rare cancer, or a cancer that came back.
  • You were offered surgery, a transplant or a treatment with serious side effects.
  • You are not sure about your diagnosis, or the treatment is not working.
  • You want to know whether a clinical trial could fit you.

What to bring

  • Pathology (biopsy) reportAsk the hospital or lab for a copy. The second doctor may also ask for the actual slides or tissue block to be sent.
  • Scan reports and imagesCT, PET or MRI reports, plus a disc or online link to the images.
  • Blood test resultsRecent results, especially blood counts and any tumor markers.
  • Treatment historySurgeries, chemotherapy, radiation or other treatment, with dates.
  • Medicine listEverything you take, including vitamins, herbs and remedies. Bringing the bottles works too.
  • Insurance card, photo ID and a referral if your plan needs oneMedi-Cal and many HMO plans need a referral for a second opinion.

Questions to ask

  1. Do you agree with my diagnosis and stage?
  2. What would you recommend, and why? Is it different from my first doctor’s plan?
  3. What is the goal of treatment — cure, control or comfort?
  4. Are there other options, including clinical trials?
  5. What happens if I wait, or choose not to have treatment?
  6. Can I keep getting treatment close to home?

Good to know

  • You can ask for an interpreter at no cost. Many clinics have Spanish-speaking staff.
  • Bring a family member or friend to listen and take notes.
  • A second opinion usually does not mean you must change doctors.
